questions.q: What is TorchDynamo's role in the `torch.compile` pipeline?
options: It traces executing Python/PyTorch code into an intermediate graph representation, without requiring the model to be rewritten
It only handles GPU memory allocation
It replaces PyTorch's autograd engine entirely
It converts the model's weights to a lower precision
questions.explain: TorchDynamo captures the sequence of tensor operations as your code actually executes, building a graph that later stages can optimize.

questions.q: What does AOTAutograd contribute to the compilation pipeline?
options: It fuses kernels into Triton code
It derives the backward-pass graph ahead of time from the traced forward graph, so both can be optimized together
It profiles the GPU's memory bandwidth
It handles pinned memory allocation
questions.explain: AOTAutograd takes the forward graph TorchDynamo captured and derives the corresponding backward graph ahead of time, rather than building it op-by-op at runtime.

questions.q: Why is the first call to a `torch.compile`-wrapped model's forward pass noticeably slower than later calls?
options: The GPU needs to warm up its fans
Compilation is triggered lazily by the first real forward pass with actual input shapes, and later calls reuse the cached compiled kernels
The first call always runs on CPU
torch.compile disables the GPU for one iteration
questions.explain: Compilation happens on first invocation with real shapes, so that call pays the compile cost; subsequent calls with the same shape reuse the compiled kernels and run fast.

questions.q: What is a 'graph break' in the context of `torch.compile`?
options: A deliberate performance optimization that speeds up every model
A point where TorchDynamo can't continue tracing (e.g. due to value-dependent control flow) and falls back to eager execution before resuming tracing afterward
An error that always crashes the program
The moment CUDA Graphs are captured
questions.explain: A graph break happens when Dynamo encounters something it can't trace, such as control flow dependent on tensor values; it runs that part eagerly, then resumes tracing.

questions.q: What does `mode="reduce-overhead"` add on top of the default `torch.compile` pipeline?
options: It disables kernel fusion entirely
It layers CUDA Graph capture on top of the compiled kernels, targeting per-kernel launch overhead specifically
It converts the model to run entirely on CPU
It forces every operation into float64 precision
questions.explain: The reduce-overhead mode combines compiled kernels with CUDA Graph capture, aimed specifically at cutting the CPU-side launch overhead from many small kernel dispatches.
